title: Energy transfers and conservation
prior_knowledge_summary: Work is energy transferred by a force through a displacement.
For a constant force acting in the direction of motion, work is calculated using W = Fs.
Displacement, velocity, force and weight may be used as supplied context, but this lesson does not develop their earlier equations.
new_learning: Track energy transfers through a defined system.
Apply conservation of energy when some energy is dissipated.
Choose a system and account for input, useful transfer and dissipation.
Use conservation to relate work and changes in energy stores.
not_yet_taught: Power or rate of energy transfer

visual_planning.style: Planned rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketches with sparse labels and purposeful colour.
visual_planning.asset_note: No note assets were created in this text-only package pass. Every figure remains planned.

blocks.heading: Can 800 J turn into only 510 J?
content: A wound-up toy receives 800 J of work. After release, measurements show that its moving parts gained 510 J. Has 290 J vanished?
Look beyond the moving parts. The gears warmed, the table warmed and sound travelled into the room. The puzzle is not whether energy disappeared, but whether our account included every transfer.
Predict where the unaccounted 290 J could be before writing an energy balance.

figure.purpose: Open with an apparent missing-energy contradiction without revealing the completed account.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a wound-up toy. Show an 800 J input arrow, a 510 J label beside moving gears, and three unlabelled outgoing arrows toward warm gears, table and sound marks. Put a question mark over the outgoing total.
figure.alt_text: A toy receives eight hundred joules, while only five hundred and ten joules are initially accounted for in moving parts.

blocks.heading: Choose the system before counting
content: An energy account needs a boundary. If the system is only the toy's moving parts, energy crosses the boundary as heating and sound. If the system includes the toy, table and nearby air, those changes remain inside the larger system.
The principle of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can be transferred between stores and across a chosen system boundary.
The boundary changes how we describe transfers, but it never changes the total account. State the system first, then list the energy entering, leaving and changing store inside it.

figure.purpose: Show how two valid system boundaries change the description but not conservation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison. Left boundary encloses only a toy and has heat and sound arrows crossing outward. Right boundary encloses toy, table and nearby air, with the same arrows ending inside. Label both totals 800 J without filling the individual outgoing amounts.
figure.alt_text: A small and a large system boundary classify the same heat and sound transfers differently.

blocks.heading: Build an energy account
content: For a process with one measured input, conservation can be written in words: energy transferred into the system equals the total increase in energy stores plus energy transferred out of the system.

Return to the toy. The input is 800 J and the measured moving-store increase is 510 J. The remaining transfer is 800 - 510 = 290 J. That 290 J may be shared between heating and sound, but it must still appear in the complete account.
A quick check is to add every output and store increase. Their total must equal the input for the chosen start and end states.

figure.purpose: Turn conservation into a reusable input-output account.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper balance strip. Put 800 J input on the left and 510 J moving-store increase plus 290 J heating-and-sound transfer on the right. Use blocks whose widths add to the same total and a balanced scale symbol.
figure.alt_text: An eight-hundred-joule input balances a five-hundred-and-ten-joule store increase and a two-hundred-and-ninety-joule transfer.

blocks.heading: Dissipated does not mean destroyed
content: It is tempting to call heating or sound lost energy. That feels reasonable because this energy is no longer in the store we wanted and is harder to use again.
The word lost fails if it suggests destruction. Dissipated energy has been transferred to less useful, more spread-out stores, often the thermal stores of objects and surroundings.
In a brake test, 640 J leaves the moving system. If the brake and wheel gain 570 J and sound carries 70 J away, the account is 640 = 570 + 70. The useful motion ended, but the energy did not.

figure.purpose: Correct the idea that dissipated energy has disappeared.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper correction panel. Cross out a fading 640 J arrow labelled disappeared. Beside it show 640 J splitting into 570 J warming brake and wheel and 70 J sound, with a complete equality underneath.
figure.alt_text: Energy removed from motion is accounted for by heating and sound rather than disappearing.

blocks.heading: Follow a transfer through two stages
content: A workshop cart receives 1.50 kJ of work from a pull. During the pull, its chosen moving store increases by 1.08 kJ. The track and wheels gain 0.42 kJ in their thermal stores. The first-stage check is 1.50 = 1.08 + 0.42 kJ.

The cart then enters a padded stop. Its 1.08 kJ moving-store energy is transferred again: 0.96 kJ increases thermal and deformation stores in the pad and cart, while 0.12 kJ is carried away by sound. The second-stage check is 1.08 = 0.96 + 0.12 kJ.

Carry the shared value with its unit from one stage to the next. Across the whole process, the original 1.50 kJ input becomes 0.42 + 0.96 + 0.12 = 1.50 kJ. This whole-route check is independent of either single-stage subtraction.

symbols: W is the work done, which is the energy transferred by the force.
F is the constant force acting in the direction of the displacement.
s is the displacement in the direction of the force.
formula_to_remember.units: W is measured in joules, J; F in newtons, N; and s in metres, m.

figure.purpose: Model a two-stage energy chain with a carried intermediate value and whole-route check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flow diagram. Stage 1: 1.50 kJ work splits into 1.08 kJ cart motion and 0.42 kJ thermal. Carry 1.08 kJ into Stage 2, splitting to 0.96 kJ pad and cart stores and 0.12 kJ sound. End with the whole-route sum.
figure.alt_text: A one-point-five-kilojoule input is tracked through cart motion and then into thermal, deformation and sound transfers.

blocks.heading: A reliable conservation routine
content: Choose the start and end states. Draw the system boundary. List energy entering, energy leaving and every stated store change. Use one unit throughout. Write the balance before subtracting, then check that both sides total the same amount.

When a force and displacement are supplied, work W = Fs may provide the input transfer. When later-topic energy changes are supplied as numbers, use those numbers directly without importing formulas that have not yet been taught.

Stop at this lesson's boundary. We can conserve and account for energy, including dissipation, but we have not learned named gravitational or kinetic energy equations, efficiency, power, elastic-energy formulas or variable-force integration.

figure.purpose: Compress system choice, accounting and checking into a reusable procedure.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper six-step flow strip: choose states, draw boundary, list transfers, use one unit, balance, check totals. Include one small warning card saying use supplied later-topic changes only.
figure.alt_text: A six-step checklist for selecting a system and completing an energy-conservation account.

concepts_taught: Energy conservation within a chosen system
Energy transfers across a system boundary
Dissipation as transfer to less useful stores
misconceptions_addressed: Changing the system boundary changes whether energy is conserved.
next_lesson_can_assume: Choose and state a system boundary.
